title: The dog's ten loudest barks
allegory: Reading max activating examples is like working out what a dog barks at from its ten loudest barks of the year: vivid and useful, but it describes the dog's most extreme moments, not most of its barking.
map: a latent (or neuron) you want to understand
the latent's activation on each token
the ten loudest barks from a year of recordings
the top-k max activating examples from a corpus
all the quieter barks you never listened to
the rest of the activation distribution, where most firings live
predicting next week's barks from your theory, then checking
scoring an explanation by predicting activations on held-out text

cap.1: You pull a feature out of a model and have no idea what it means. The obvious first move: find the moments it fires hardest, and read them.
cap.2: Run a big corpus through the model, record the latent's activation on every token, keep the top-k contexts and read them. It is the first panel everyone looks at.
cap.3: Max activating examples: the top-k (sequence, position) pairs by a latent's activation over a corpus, shown with context and per-token values. The cheapest hypothesis generator.

cap.1: Picture working out what a dog barks at from its ten loudest barks of the year. All ten are at the postman. So it barks at the postman?
cap.2: Top examples are the extreme upper tail of the activation distribution. They are vivid and easy to label, and that is exactly why they can mislead.
cap.3: Top-k selection samples the extreme tail, so incidental context shared by the strongest firings is indistinguishable from the true trigger without further evidence.

curves.label: how often it fires at each strength

cap.1: Line up every bark by loudness. Most are fairly quiet. The ten loudest sit far out on the right, a sliver of the dog's day.
cap.2: Most of a latent's firings are mid or low strength. Top-k examples come from the far tail, so an explanation built from them describes the tail, not the body.
cap.3: An explanation fitted to top-k describes the upper tail; the latent's mid- and low-activation behaviour, which is most of its firings, never enters the evidence.

chapters.name: The illusion
chapters.verdict: Top examples make almost any latent look meaningful. Check before you name it.

cap.1: 'Barks at the postman' sounds perfect, until you record next week and the dog barks at squirrels, the doorbell and the kettle.
cap.2: Top examples make almost any latent look meaningful. ARENA pairs them with the activation distribution and the latent's logit effects instead of trusting them alone.
cap.3: The interpretability illusion: a crisp top-k label can score near chance on held-out text. Sample across activation quantiles, include non-firing contexts, check logit effects.

cap.1: The fix is a test: write your theory down, predict where it fires on text it has never seen, then check. A good theory predicts; a pretty one only describes.
cap.2: Autointerp does this at scale: one model writes an explanation from top examples, another predicts activations on fresh text from that explanation alone. The score is the metric.
cap.3: OpenAI (2023) explained all 307,200 GPT-2 neurons this way: over a thousand scored ≥ 0.8, the vast majority scored poorly. Score, not readability, measures interpretability.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Top examples: a great first guess
Density, logits, fresh text: before you name it
Unscored labels get cited as facts

cap.1: Top examples are how you get a first guess about any feature. Treat that guess as a question, not an answer.
cap.2: Form a hypothesis from top examples, then test it with the activation density, the latent's effect on outputs, and predictions on fresh text. That is the dashboard's whole design.
cap.3: Steer a model with a mislabelled feature and you steer it somewhere you did not intend: labels must be scored against held-out behaviour before they carry weight.

coda.title: A dog with a rare loud trigger and a common quiet one. Where do you stop listening?

readouts.label: postman's share of what you read
readouts.f: round(100 * share * sigmoid(3.404 * (loud - cut)) / ((1 - share) * sigmoid(3.404 * (2 - cut)) + share * sigmoid(3.404 * (loud - cut)))) + '%'

readouts.label: barks you actually read
readouts.f: round(1000 * ((1 - share) * sigmoid(3.404 * (2 - cut)) + share * sigmoid(3.404 * (loud - cut)))) / 10 + '%'

caption.1: Slide the cut right so you read only the loudest barks: soon they are all postman, though most barks are squirrels. Slide it left to hear the whole dog.
caption.2: This latent has a rare strong trigger and a common weak one. A high cut, like top-k, sees only the rare one. Lowering it, like sampling across quantiles, reveals both.
caption.3: Top-k conditions on the extreme tail, so a rare high-activation mode dominates the evidence even when a common low-activation mode dominates the firings.

where_else: Autointerp: a language model writing, then scoring, explanations built from these examples
Feature dashboards on Neuronpedia: top examples beside density, logit effects and explanations
Survivorship bias: judging a strategy by its most famous winners

hamming.what: The corpus inputs where a latent fires hardest, read to form a first guess at what it means.
hamming.when: As the first look at any new neuron or SAE latent, always alongside its activation density, logit effects and a scored prediction.
hamming.why: They are the fastest way to a hypothesis and the fastest way to fool yourself, because they only show the extreme tail.

object.title: The far island
object.subtitle: Every dot is one moment of text; the latent grows louder to the right. You only read the island past the sheet.

plane.label: the top-k cut: you only read beyond here

cap.1: Every dot is one moment in the text. The further right, the harder the feature fires.
cap.2: Each point is a token context; the x-direction is the latent's activation.
cap.3: Contexts placed by the latent's activation along x; the other axes are arbitrary context variation.

cap.1: The sheet is where you stop reading. Only the small island beyond it makes your top ten, and it all looks alike.
cap.2: Top-k reading keeps only contexts past the cut: a small, tight, unrepresentative group.
cap.3: Selection on the extreme tail yields a homogeneous sample, which makes a crisp label easy and uninformative.

cap.1: Behind the sheet sits the big crowd of quieter firings, the ones your label never heard about.
cap.2: Most firings are mid or low strength and never reach the top-k list.
cap.3: The body of the activation distribution carries most of the latent's behaviour and is absent from top-k evidence.

cap.1: From above: a tiny bright island far out, a big continent near home. The label came from the island.
cap.2: An explanation fitted to the island may say nothing true about the continent.
cap.3: Explanation quality must be measured on samples drawn across the distribution, not on the selection that produced it.

cap.1: Checking a label means sampling the continent too, and predicting fresh text before you trust it.
cap.2: Sample across activation strengths, include text where it never fires, and score predictions on held-out text.
cap.3: Quantile sampling plus held-out predictive scoring (autointerp) converts a tail description into a tested claim about the latent.

predict.q: A latent's top 20 examples are all legal contracts. What do you actually know?

options.t: What its strongest firings look like, not what most of its firings are
That it is a legal-contracts feature

predict.why: Top examples are the extreme tail. Most firings are weaker and may be about something else.

predict.q: What is the best test of the label 'fires on legal terms'?

options.t: Predict where it fires on fresh text, then compare with the real activations
Read more of the top examples

predict.why: Only predictions on held-out text show whether the label describes the latent, not just its top examples.

predict.q: OpenAI scored GPT-4's explanations of all 307,200 GPT-2 neurons. How did most do?

options.t: Most scored poorly; over a thousand scored 0.8 or better

predict.why: Readable explanations are easy to write and predictive ones are rare, which is why the scoring half matters.

object.where: Anywhere a highlight reel stands in for the whole: top examples, famous winners, five-star reviews.
